name: Carla Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we aren't selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's full, and I like it full. I'm studying computer science, so there are lectures and labs, and I'm in the library most evenings. Two nights a week I work in the phone support team for a broadband company, and on Sundays after church I lead the youth group, about twelve teenagers. I share a flat with two girls from church, and I use AI tools every day, for planning, for code, for everything.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Loud, and I love it. We do a Bible study and then pizza, and last month I got the teenagers to build a small website for the church food drive using an AI assistant. They were so proud. My mum says I'm the only person she knows who can pray and debug in the same hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, a little less noise. I'd still say we should learn the tools, because even small gains help, but nobody needs to panic. I'd say it in the church group, and I'd say we should be thankful and get on with our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be calm. My degree keeps its value, my parents keep their jobs, and my plans stay the same. Mum is a pharmacist and Dad is an accountant, and in a world where AI mostly doesn't change things, they both have years of steady work ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep the support job for the money, because it pays for my books and my share of the flat. I'd keep leading the youth group, and I'd apply for a summer internship with a software firm. And I'd keep using AI, since it helps me learn faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and grateful. I know I'm fortunate. Family helps with fees, I've got a job, and I'm doing what I wanted to do since I was fourteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the chatbot at the support job helps a bit. What does it change in your shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The support job is the one place I'd notice a bit of change. The company has a chatbot that answers simple questions, and it saves us time on easy ones. In this world, that's about all it does, and I'm fine with it. It lets me spend more time on the callers who really need help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad likes to say that the world will always need people to count the money and people to give out the medicine. In this version, he's right. I'd put my worry somewhere else, like my brother Chidi's exams.

say: I'd say **good**, a little less noise, and we should still learn the tools.
I'd say we should be **thankful** and get on with our work.
think: I'd be **calm**: my degree keeps its value and my parents keep their jobs.
I know I'm **fortunate** with family help and a job.
do: Keep the **support job** for books and flat money.
S0.quote: The world will always need people to count the money and people to give out the medicine.
fieldNote: Carla is **calm and grateful**, and she speaks with an easy confidence.
She sees AI in the support job as a small help that frees time for callers who need people.
Her parents' jobs, pharmacist and accountant, are secure **mild world only**.

steps.text: Keep the two evening support shifts each week
Apply for a software internship in the spring
Use AI to plan study weeks and check code

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a time to work hard and look after each other. If AI does the thinking jobs, we shouldn't wait for the government to fix it. Families, churches and employers should help people retrain, and people should be ready to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd worry about my parents more than myself. Mum checks prescriptions and Dad does accounts, and both are checking and paperwork. In this world, those are exactly the tasks that go to software. They both still have work, but fewer people would be hired, and Dad's firm might cut a few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean in. I'd become the person in my family who understands the tools, and I'd teach Mum and Dad. I'd take modules where I'd build things, not just write code. And I'd keep the support job, since the callers who need a human voice aren't going away soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for them. It's a funny feeling, being 18 and thinking about how to protect your parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about your parents more than yourself. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The support job is where I'd see it first. The company will use chatbots for more and more calls, and the team will shrink. I'd probably get fewer shifts. So I'd need more tutoring to make up the money, and I've got a couple of students lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach them first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents to put some money aside. When my parents say not to worry them, I'd say I'm not worried, I'm preparing. That's the truth, and it's easier for them to hear.

say: I'd say it's a time to **work hard**, not to wait for government.
I'd say churches and employers should help people **retrain**.
think: Mum's **prescription checks** and Dad's accounts are exactly the tasks that go to software.
Dad's firm might **cut a few** people, though both still have work.
do: Become the family's **tools expert** and teach Mum and Dad.
Take modules where I **build things**, not only write code.
Add **tutoring** to replace lost support shifts.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for my parents than for me.
S1.quote: When my parents say not to worry them, I'd say I'm not worried, I'm preparing.
fieldNote: Carla's worry is for her **parents' paperwork jobs**, a precise, personal exposure.
She frames protection of family as her role, which fits her **traditional** values.
She expects her own support shifts to shrink and plans tutoring to fill the gap.

steps.text: Teach Mum and Dad two AI tools at the weekend
Ask my parents to set aside an emergency fund
Take on two extra maths and coding tutoring students
Save a month of pay each term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's pray and let's plan, in that order. Two years is shockingly short, and I'd say the people building it owe us honesty. I'd say it in church, and I'd tell my friends to hold their families close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened for my parents. Mum's and Dad's jobs are thinking jobs. If AI can do almost any thinking work in 2028, they could both be out of work within a couple of years. I'd be thinking about my brother's school fees and my own, and I'd be alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Mum and Dad and make a real budget, not a pretend one. I'd stop spending on anything extra. I'd work more shifts at the support job, while it exists, and take on tutoring. And I'd stay on my course, because I'd have nothing else ready, but I'd start looking at what's practical, like healthcare technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night doing sums. It's a very specific fear: both parents' jobs, my fees, my brother's school, all hitting at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit down with your parents and make a real budget. What would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my family's strength is that we pray and plan together. Dad would hate asking for help, but the church has people who've been through job losses. I'd make sure he talked to them. Pride shouldn't get in the way of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your dad feel about asking the church for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say to Mum that pharmacy has a hands-on side, with counters and customers, and that might last a bit longer. I'd say it softly, since I don't want to give her false hope. It's a small piece of hope that's true.

say: I'd say **pray** and **plan**, in that order.
I'd tell friends to **hold their families close** and not blame each other.
think: Mum's and Dad's jobs are **thinking jobs** and could both go within a couple of years.
I'd be doing sums about my brother's **school fees** and my own.
do: Make a real **family budget** with Mum and Dad.
Work more **support shifts** and take on tutoring.
Stay on the course and look at **healthcare technology**.
S2.quote: My family's strength is that we pray and plan together.
fieldNote: Carla's alarm is **specific**: two exposed parents, her fees and her brother's school at once.
She is honest about her father's **pride** and wants him to accept church help.
She offers her mum a small, true hope about the hands-on side of pharmacy.

steps.text: Make a full family budget with Mum and Dad
Stop all spending beyond rent, food and travel
Take extra support shifts and tutoring students
Ask Dad to talk to church members who lost jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we should use it well. I'd tell the youth group to learn to work with the tools and to keep their faith and families strong. I'd say it with energy, because people listen to energy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but organised. My parents would have about five years, and Dad would be maybe two years from the age he'd planned to retire. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two working years before the thinking work is gone, so I'd want to be earning well by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, go into a job with a company that builds things with AI, and pay down any debt. I'd help my parents plan their retirement a little earlier, if they can. And I'd keep the youth group going, because that's what keeps me grounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd say it's a managed anxiety. I'd feel like I'm carrying a heavy bag, but I know how to carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad might want to retire earlier. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also think about my brother, Chidi. He's fifteen, and he'd be finishing school as everything shifts. I'd want to help him choose something with people in it, like nursing or teaching, but I wouldn't push, because he's stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you help your brother Chidi decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing that surprises me is how much I think about family before myself. I think that's how I was raised. You take care of your people first, and then yourself.

say: I'd say five years is **a window** and we should use it well.
I'd tell the youth group to **work with the tools** and keep faith and families strong.
think: I'd feel **anxious but organised**, with about five years for my parents.
I'd want to be **earning well** within two working years.
do: Finish the degree and join a company that **builds with AI**.
Help my parents plan an **earlier retirement** if possible.
feel: **Anxious**, a managed anxiety, like a heavy bag I know how to carry.
S3.quote: You take care of your people first, and then yourself.
fieldNote: Carla's reflex is to **plan for family first**, and she says this is how she was raised.
She describes her anxiety as **managed**, with a bag she knows how to carry.
She wants to guide her brother Chidi towards people-centred work without pushing.

steps.text: Apply to companies that build products with AI
Pay down loan debt in the first working year
Help Mum and Dad plan an earlier retirement
Keep learning new AI tools through the youth group projects

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing, and it's for building. I'd tell people not to waste it on worry. I'd say that we should learn, save and help each other, and I'd say it with a smile because I mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel much better. Ten years means I could finish my degree, work for a few years, and start a project of my own. My parents would be near retirement, and maybe the changes would reach them just as they step back, which would be a mercy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at a software firm, and build a side project, maybe an app for church communities. I'd save and put money into something steady, like a house. And I'd help my brother and maybe my parents with some of what they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with hope. A long timeline gives me time to prepare, but I know how fast these things can speed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a business with friends from church. What would it build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably start a small business with some friends from church. We trust each other, and that matters. We'd build tools for community groups, like food banks, youth clubs and congregations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would making it kinder mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, there's a part of me that wants to be one of the people who shapes it. I'm good with the tools, and I'm good with people. I'd like to be the person who makes it kinder.

say: I'd say ten years is **a blessing** and meant for building.
I'd tell people not to **waste it on worry**.
think: I'd feel **much better**, with time to finish, work and start a project.
The changes might reach my parents **after** they step back, which would be a mercy.
do: Finish the degree and work at a **software firm**.
Build an **app for church communities** on the side.
Put money into something steady, like a **house**.
feel: **Uneasy**, with hope, because things can speed up.
S4.quote: I'd like to be the person who makes it kinder.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets Carla **plan to shape change**, not only survive it.
Her business idea stays rooted in **church and community trust**.
She keeps a note of caution: she knows how fast things can speed up.

steps.text: Finish the computer science degree and a graduate job
Build an app for church food banks and youth clubs
Save a house deposit within seven years
Help Chidi and my parents with fees and bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, because both my parents' jobs are thinking jobs and my family would have no time to prepare. What would help is honest warning from companies and the government, and support for families to retrain together. Also, churches and communities need to be ready to help, because they will be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think young Christians like me are afraid of new technology. I'm not. I think new tools are a gift, and the question is whether we use them to look after each other.

headlineQuote: I think new tools are a gift, and the question is whether we use them to look after each other.
portrait: Carla is an **18-year-old** computer science student who works evenings in phone support and leads a church youth group.
Her mum is a pharmacist and her dad an accountant, so both parents' jobs are **thinking work**.
She is traditional and adaptive, uses AI **every day** and teaches others to use it.
Her moods are calm in the mild world and **alarmed** in the two-year one, because her family is exposed.
She puts **family first**, plans with prayer and budgets, and dreams of making technology kinder.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries her most, because both parents' jobs would go and nobody could prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest warning**, support for families to retrain together and ready church communities.
